blocks.content: --network none gives a container no network access at all, beyond a bare loopback interface. It is the most restrictive networking mode Docker offers.

A container started with --network none has just a loopback interface (127.0.0.1), useful only for a process talking to itself, it has no bridge connection, no assigned IP reachable by anything else, nothing.

blocks.alt: Just loopback, nothing that reaches outward

blocks.content: This is not a soft restriction, a container in this mode cannot reach the internet, cannot reach other containers, cannot be reached from outside, there is no network path in or out at all beyond the container's own loopback.

blocks.alt: No path in, no path out, at all

blocks.content: 3. Where This Is the Right Choice
blocks.text: 3. Where This Is the Right Choice

blocks.content: This mode fits workloads that genuinely have no legitimate need for network access, an isolated data-processing job reading and writing only local files, for instance, where removing network access entirely is a real, meaningful security boundary rather than just an inconvenience.

blocks.alt: A real security boundary for workloads that need no network at all

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: None network mode strips a container down to loopback only, no connectivity in or out beyond talking to itself.
It is a deliberate security choice for workloads with no legitimate need for any network access, not a default setting.
